To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the majority of T lymphocytes in the human tuberculin reaction have an helper/inducer phenotype, and that these cells appose HLA-DR+ antigen presenting cells.
T lymphocytes of the 'helper/inducer type' are involved in the tuberculin reaction, and that they are closely apposed to HLA- DR expressing cells in the dermis and epidermis.

T lymphocytes of the 'helper/inducer phenotype' are the predominant cells in the tuberculin reaction, that they appose to HLA-Dr expressing cells and that this reaction is a morphologic correlate of in vitro experiments on proliferation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the cellular elements involved in the tuberculin reactions in human skin.
the development of a new method to study cell-mediated immune reactions.
the development of a new technique of double staining of immunocytochemically labelled cells in tissue sections.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the T lymphocyte subset pattern of the tuberculin reaction in man is similar to that of the tubercle bacilli in the skin of guinea pigs and that the T lymphocytes of the 'helper' subset are the major effector cells in this type of immune reaction.
the T lymphocytes in the skin tuberculin reactions are predominantly of the 'helper/inducer type', and are in close contact with HLA-DR positive cells, probably monocytes/macrophages.
in the human skin reaction to tuberculin, the T lymphocyte subsets Leu 3 and Leu 2 are involved, and that these cells are in close contact with HLA-DR cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the T lymphocyte subsets are differentially distributed within the dermis and epidermis and that these cells are in close apposition with HLA-DR positive cells.

the tuberculin reaction in human skin is a complex reaction with a number of cell populations, which are activated and migrate into the dermis and the epidermis, where they interact with HLA-DR bearing cells.
in the human skin reaction to tuberculin, the majority of the T cells are of 'helper' phenotype, and that the 'helper' cells interact with HLA-DR positive cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the immune system is a dynamic system that is always on the move.
the skin is a good model system for studying the cellular immune response.
the skin tuberculin test is a useful model to study the interaction between T lymphocytes and HLA-Dr positive cells in delayed type hypersensitivity.
